title: Callistus (14 October)
hook: a slave who lost his master's money, worked the mines, and became bishop of Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, Denis, and the hill of Montmartre. Your line was the mountain of martyrs.

A slave in Rome is trusted with his master's money. He runs a kind of bank, and other Christians deposit their savings with him. Then the money is gone. He panics and runs. He's caught, punished, and later sent to labor in the mines of Sardinia. On any list of future popes, his name would not appear. And yet some years later, the man from the mines is bishop of Rome. Today, Callistus.
screen: `A SLAVE WITH A BANK.` → `THE MONEY IS GONE.` → `FROM THE MINES TO ROME.`

segments.voice: Much of what we know about Callistus comes from someone who disliked him: Hippolytus, a Roman priest and writer who opposed him bitterly. So read the story with that in mind. The bank failure, the flight, the mines: Hippolytus tells it to make Callistus look bad. Some readers today come away liking Callistus more. Released from Sardinia, he lived quietly outside Rome for a time; later the bishop of Rome, Zephyrinus, took him in, made him a deacon, and put him in charge of the Christian burial ground on the Appian Way. Those underground galleries still bear his name: the Catacombs of Saint Callistus. Then he was chosen bishop of Rome himself. Here's what made Hippolytus so angry. Callistus allowed Christians who had committed serious sins, and had done penance, to be welcomed back to communion. Hippolytus thought that was far too soft. Cornelius would face the same question after him. Some readers see Callistus's own story in his answer: a man who had failed with other people's money, been punished, and been given a second chance, now keeping the door open for others. In Matthew, Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive. Seven times? The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Tradition says Callistus died a martyr. And tradition says Hippolytus, in time, was reconciled to the Church and also died a martyr. The Church now honors them both as saints. The angry critic and the forgiving shepherd ended up on the same calendar.
screen: `HIS STORY COMES FROM A RIVAL.` · `KEEPER OF THE CATACOMBS.` · `HE WELCOMED BACK THOSE WHO REPENTED.` · `BOTH MEN BECAME SAINTS.` · then, large: `SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: Think of a person who let you or others down and has tried to make it right, and notice whether there's a door in you still shut against them. You don't have to fling it open; just see if it could open a crack. If you pray, bring them before God by name; if you don't, simply picture greeting them warmly, once.
Callistus. A slave who failed, was punished, came back, kept the catacombs, and as bishop of Rome welcomed back sinners who repented.
Your line: from slave to shepherd. A second chance, passed on to others. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Pope Saint Callistus I is remembered on 14 October; in Rome, pilgrims visit the Catacombs of Saint Callistus on the Appian Way.

chat.says: How did a runaway slave who lost people's money end up as pope?
options: Bishop Zephyrinus took him in and made him a deacon; later he was chosen bishop of Rome.
He paid back every coin from the mines, and the Romans elected him out of gratitude.
His master freed him and bought him the office, as rich families did then.
chat.meaning: After the mines, Zephyrinus took Callistus in and made him a deacon; later chosen bishop of Rome, he kept the door open for repentant sinners.

Sardinia.meaning: the island where he labored in the mines

Zephyrinus.meaning: the bishop of Rome who made him a deacon

Appian Way.meaning: an old Roman road, by the burial ground he kept

Catacombs.meaning: underground burial galleries, these named for him

Hippolytus.meaning: the rival priest who told his story
